research.query: Which materials are most flammable in microgravity?
research.answer:
The question was matched to: microgravity, material flammability. Below is what the indexed documents state about it, quoted with their sources.

**Evidence**
- SAFFIRE-II: Flammability of several spacecraft materials in microgravity compared side-by-side with 1-g reference burns of the same samples. [S1]
- SAFFIRE-I: gravity material flammability screening test. [S2]
- BASS-II: 2) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. [S3]
- ACME BRE: This could enable the Cone Calorimeter (NASA Test 2) test as a basis for establishing flammability maps for real materials. [S4]
- BASS-II: concentration, temperature, etc.). NASA tests and controls materials from a flammability perspective using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for [S5]
- Dust can look like smoke to a particle counter: DAFT showed that a modified commercial particle counter could be used in microgravity, measuring a test dust aerosol released on the ISS. Limitation: Terrestrial test dust, not lunar regolith; feasibility test only. [S10]
- BASS-II maps solid-fuel burning down to 13.6 % O2: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. Limitation: Outcome annotations  [S11]

**Limits**
- Extractive answer (no language model configured): passages are quoted, not interpreted.
- Only documents in this knowledge base were searched.

sources.title: BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids — insight:bass-1g-screening-gap
sources.text: 1-g material screening is not automatically conservative. Spacecraft material selection relies on NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, which ranks materials by 1-g behaviour. BASS and BASS-II were built on the hypothesis that, with adequate ventilation, materials burn as well if not better in microgravity than in normal gravity. Which flow speeds and flow directions must a microgravity-relevant material test include?

sources.title: BASS — Burning and Suppression of Solids — hypothesis
sources.text: BASS experiments were based on the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.) To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft.

sources.title: SAFFIRE-II — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II — insight:saffire2-ug-vs-1g
sources.text: Microgravity and 1-g rankings of materials can disagree. In SAFFIRE-II, 4 of 4 silicone samples (0.27–1.03 mm) had a burn length of about 0 in microgravity at 20 cm/s, while 2 of the 4 matching 1-g reference burns were complete. Flames did spread in microgravity over: PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric). A 1-g screening result can be optimistic for some materials (BASS hypothesis) and pessimistic for others — which materials of a given vehicle need microgravity testing?

sources.title: SAFFIRE-III — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III — objective
sources.text: (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.

sources.title: Cool flames: combustion at 500–1000 K
sources.text: Cool diffusion flames have peak temperatures of about 500–1000 K. FLEX, CFI and CFI-G studied them on droplets and burners in microgravity. Limitation: Research fuels and configurations; relevance to cabin fires is an open question, not a finding.
